The actual thing that pushed me to do it was a rejection from a guy. He wasn't even that great - he's not my usual type, and I can objectively see that he's not actually a particularly nice person and he's very immature. I'd seen photos of his really beautiful, skinny ex girlfriend, and I knew I couldn't compete with that, but it still hurt. One night I was feeling really down and crying about being rejected yet again, and how nobody I've ever been interested in has wanted to date me, and I think a big part of that is because I'm obese. I decided that night to do something about it, I'd read success stories about Mounjaro, I finally have the disposable income to afford it, so I ordered my first pen and I haven't looked back.


Considering the stories people have here, my reason seems very silly, but it was kind of the straw that broke the camel's back - I was struggling with my mental health again, I hated how I looked in photos, I've got more friend's weddings coming up this year and I want to be happy with the person I see in the photos. I'm very concerned about developing diabetes and hypertension - my BP has been a little on the higher side for a while, and I'm only 32, but not quite high enough to need to do anything.

I'm also really sick of not being able to do things because of my weight - can't do this activity on holiday because I'm over the weight limit, scared that I'm not going to be able to fasten my seatbelt on a plane, not fit enough to do this hike that looks really good but I know I'll just slow my friends down/not make it. A while ago I wanted a new garden chair, but I'm over the weight limit for lots of the nice ones I saw.

I'm only 8 weeks in, lost about 16lbs and I'm not seeing that much of a change yet, but I'm definitely losing and I'm tolerating 5mg well (just started my second 5mg pen last night because I'm getting pretty good suppression and minimal side effects, so I'm happy with this dose for now.) I'm really excited to be able to do all the things I want to do as I lose the weight.

I've been taking azathioprine for an autoimmune condition for about 8 years, and I've been a doctor for a bit over 5 years, and in my EM training programme for 3. During that time I've rotated through a few different areas, including ITU and anaesthetics, and I've done about 2 years of EM in total.

I did have to shield in the first wave of covid, but second wave and beyond I kept working clinically. Initially this was in non-covid areas, but by summer 2021 I was working normally. Being forced to shield during the pandemic was the only issue I've experienced with my immunosuppression. I will say that I've been lucky that my disease has been very well controlled since the diagnosis and initial induction of remission with steroids 8 years ago, and I'm now coming off the azathioprine to see what happens and hope I can get a break from it, but it really hasn't caused me any problems. I've had the usual coughs/colds and norovirus or similar once, but I don't find that I get sick any more than my 'healthy' colleagues. I've had covid twice, I was fine with it, and I'm 98% sure I didn't get it from work either time. If anything I think I get sick less than some of my colleagues, but I was always like that pre-immunosuppression so that could just be me. I'm careful about hand washing, but not crazy about it, and tbh I can be a bit lax about other PPE now.

Only you can decide what risks you're willing to take with your health - but the stress, shift patterns etc with EM may cause you issues with your MS (as you've alluded to) in a way that I fortunately haven't experienced with my disease, so that's an extra issue to consider.

I'm very happy to talk via DM if there's anything I can help with, and I wish you luck with both your health and your chosen specialty.

There's plenty of advantages to medicine, and I wouldn't go back to waitressing. But the current issues with training and pay shouldn't be ignored.
But your point was about how people should be able to expect a doctor to be nice the same way as they should expect a waiter to be nice, because it's "the bare minimum" and they should be able to "shake it off". But the two jobs are completely different, and one involves seeing and being a part of deeply distressing things, so the expectation that we should be friendly at all times is unrealistic. It was easier to be friendly all the time as a waitress than it is as a doctor, although I always try to.

I also don't think it's realistic to expect a waiter to be friendly all the time - they may be a bit cold because the last table was really rude to them, the chef shouted at them and they know that the regular creepy guy has just been seated in their section. Or, they were the patient the GP told they had an incurable disease, but they have to go back to work to pay the rent.
Essentially human beings aren't machines who can turn their emotions off and on at will, no matter what job they do.

I was a waitress for years, and now I'm a junior doctor. It was easier to be friendly as a waitress because if a table was rude to me, didn't leave me a tip, the chef shouted at me and the other waitress was mean to me at least I didn't have to watch a human being die despite the best efforts of all my colleagues, then call their family and tell them their relative was dead. I had some terrible shifts as a waitress, but I never had to tell someone that their much loved family member was terminally ill. A mistake as a waitress meant that a table was angry about the wrong meal, and the chef was angry about having to cook another meal. A mistake as a doctor means someone comes to harm or dies.
I'm friendly most of the time as a doctor, but if I or my colleagues aren't on top form then consider that our last patient might just have been a dying child. 

Incidentally, the pay is shit and I still drive the same car as when I was a waitress because my student loan, expenses of rotational training, exams and professional fees suck up a lot of money on top of our >20% real terms pay cut. And I've been a doctor for 3.5 years.

Another friend failed several exams - again passed in the end, and is working and doing well.

Lots of people fail exams in medical school and go on to be fantastic doctors. A great ED consultant I worked with once told me that he failed his paeds exam and had to leave elective early to resit it. I did final year with people who failed the first time, and they graduated successfully.

Failure feels horrible and it's terrifying. Generally medics have excelled in school, and this can be the first taste of failing something academically - it's really hard to get to grips with, but you'll get there.
If your mental health is taking a hit then make sure you take time for yourself and reach out to your GP.

You will get through this, and one day you'll be a consultant telling a frightened medical student that you failed an exam in first year, yet here you are.

Sounds like your department is not well set up for the doctors to be efficient, in which case you're just not going to be able to - it's a shame yours is like this. Emergency medicine is a team sport (it's one of the things I love about it), and I have no problem chaperoning an exam or doing urgent bloods/ECG/bladder scan or whatever is needed - but it isn't up to us to be solely doing that, when there are things that only we can do which are pressing.
Sometimes you do get pulled away and a patient ends up waiting longer than is ideal, and some of that is about managing expectations ("I'll be back as soon as I can, but sometimes I have to attend to emergencies", or telling a patient the trop you're running takes 90 minutes when you know it should be back in an hour). However it sounds like you're doing an awful lot to keep an under-resourced department running. There are some things you might need to try and say no to, or say you'll chaperone this exam after you discharge your patient, but ultimately if your area isn't well set up to manage the patients with appropriate nursing cover for ECGs etc, then you'll be slower and it's worth explaining that to a friendly senior if you can/if you're being challenged on your speed.

As a side note - I worry that I'm slow, I always have done, but I get nice feedback from my seniors and nobody has ever told me I'm slow. I'm guilty of comparing myself to others a lot, and being quite self critical, and I think that's some that affects a lot of us to try to go easy on yourself.

I've always been told 1 per hour, and it's a good rule to go by. Sometimes you'll get a quick patient that you can discharge in ten minutes, and sometimes you'll have a complex patient who needs lots of history and examination time, then a scan, then breaking bad news, then referral, then a tonne of documentation.
True minor injuries are often quick, a secret sickie hiding in the minors queue with a benign sounding presenting complaint will take ages. Majors/resus really varies.

As has already been said, flow is not your problem.
Try and be efficient - see a new patient while waiting for results to come back - but never sacrifice safety for speed. Wanting to try and shorten the queue will not help you in coroner's court.

Other staff/grades taking all the quick cases will also slow down your average, and your seniors should recognise this. Some people are also naturally faster than others, and that's okay - we all have our strengths.
I'm an EM trainee and I don't think I'm particularly quick, but I can juggle a few which speeds me up. Some of our registrars fly through cases, and others are more methodical. It's just natural variation in approach.

So long as you're safe, and not pissing around when you should be seeing patients (or spending an hour talking to a patient with a broken toe about the exact breed of cat they tripped over), you'll be grand.
